newsitem.title: UK: Militant Islamic rally moves to London's Hyde Park.
newsitem.headline: Militant Islamic rally moves to London's Hyde Park.

text.p: A controversial Islamic rally, condemned by some Middle Eastern states, will go ahead in London on Sunday despite an earlier cancellation, one of the organisers said on Saturday.
The rally was originally planned for a 12,000-seat arena but was called off at the last moment because of high security costs.

Instead, an organiser said, speeches will be delivered at London"s Hyde Park Corner, a traditional, open-air free speech venue that usually attracts soapbox orators, heckled by mainly good-humoured audiences.

Egypt and Algeria, both fighting internal Islamic threats, had urged Britain to ban the mass rally. But a government spokesman said neither the Home Office (interior ministry) nor the police had any powers to cancel the event.

"It may be just a press conference because it has been arranged at such short notice, but hopefully some of the thousands of people who had booked seats will be there," Saudi dissident, Mohammed al-Masari told Reuters by telephone.
Masari said he and militant Syrian Omar Bakri-Mohammed, who has called for a worldwide Islamic state, would address a crowd at Speaker's Corner (0930 GMT)
Bakri-Mohammed's al-Muhajiroun group had planned to hold its "Rally for Revival" at the London Arena in the east of the British capital.
It was called off at the last moment because the organisation was asked to pay thousands of pounds (dollars) for extra security after foreign governments urged Britain to ban the meeting.
Britain warned the organisers that it would not tolerate statements supporting terrorism, but said it had no powers to prevent the meeting.
Al-Muhajiroun has called for a Holy War against Middle East governments.
Police said they were not aware that the meeting had been moved, but said the organisers did not have to ask for permission to hold a rally at Speakers' Corner.
Moslem academics and representatives from Islamic movements around the world had planned to attend the original one-day rally.

Militant Islamic leaders including Omar Abdul-Rahman, the 65-year-old sheikh jailed for life in the bombing of the World Trade Centre in New York, were also due to address the conference in pre-recorded videos.
A British gay rights group said it would hold a rival rally at Speaker's Corner in protest at al-Muhajiroun's call for the death penalty on homosexuals.
"I am surprised at the holding of such a conference which will include many of those elements who encourage terrrorism," Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak said in Cairo of the planned mass rally.
Algeria described the rally as "a meeting bringing together masterminds and ideologists and financers of terrorism."
Jewish groups in Britain have also voiced their concern.
London is seen in some overseas capitals as an overly tolerant city towards dissident groups, especially those with their roots in the Middle East.
It is home to tens of thousands of Moslem expatriates, many opposition groups have their headquarters in London and several Arab and Islamic newspapers are published here.
